student.question: Who is the service owner of the decision on closed tickets and reopening?
student.answer: The service owner of the decision on closed tickets and reopening is The Incident Manager, process owner of incident management. Source: [DECISIONS.md]
student.context:
[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening
**Decision:** A closed ticket is immutable. Reopen works from resolved only, within 7 days of resolved_at; a
reopen request on a closed ticket answers 409 whatever its age, and further work on the same issue is a new
ticket that references the closed one via related_to. The minimal conflicting part of R-10, the words "or
closed" and "or closure", is rejected; reopening a resolved ticket, the rest of R-10, stands together with all
of R-09.

**Rejected alternative:** Reopen allowed from closed as well, within 7 days of closed_at, with the record
becoming immutable only after that window.

[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening
**Reason:** Closure is the point where the record becomes evidence: it feeds SLA attainment reports, problem
records and the monthly service review, and a record that can silently change after that point makes every
report reproducible only by luck. The 7-day reopen window after resolution already gives the reporter the "the
fix did not work" path that R-10 is for; the resolved state exists precisely so that closure can wait until
the reporter has confirmed. A new ticket linked via related_to preserves the history of both records and gives
problem management a countable signal, how many closed tickets spawned follow-up work, instead of a mutated
one.

**Service owner:** The Incident Manager, process owner of incident management, who signs off the closure rules
because closure is what makes the incident record trustworthy for reporting and problem management.

**Customer outcome:** A reporter whose fix failed within a week reopens the resolved ticket without friction;
once the ticket is closed, the customer raises a linked ticket and the history of both is preserved, so the
reports the customer relies on (SLA attainment, recurring issues) stay true.

[specs/spec.md]
Feature specification: svcdesk, the service-desk API > Functional requirements
  `paused` evaluated at the request's `now`; equality is not a breach; a reopened ticket is unresolved again
  and keeps its resolution target (R-15, R-16).
- FR-5 State machine (R-07, R-08): ack from new, start from acknowledged, resolve from in_progress, close from
  resolved, reopen from resolved within 7 days of `resolved_at` and, under C2 = reopen only, from closed within
  7 days of `closed_at` (R-09, R-10, R-11). Everything else is 409 with an `error` object; unknown ids are 404.
- FR-6 `GET /tickets` returns every matching ticket in one array, optionally filtered by `state` and
  `priority`, without pagination (R-19); `GET /tickets/{id}` returns one ticket or 404 (R-18).

student.question: Under the rejected alternative, when would a P1 raised on Friday at 17:00 be due for acknowledgement?
student.answer: Under the rejected alternative, a P1 raised on Friday at 17:00 would be due for acknowledgement on Monday at 08:15. Source: [DECISIONS.md]
student.context:
[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C1 - SLA clock for P1
**Decision:** P1 acknowledgement (15 min) and resolution (4 h) run on the wall clock, around the clock; P2 to
P4 targets pause outside business hours (Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 16:00 Europe/Warsaw). The minimal
conflicting part of R-13, the words "any SLA target", is narrowed to "any P2 to P4 target"; the rest of R-13
and all of R-14 stand.

**Rejected alternative:** Every priority, including P1, pauses outside business hours, so that a P1 raised on
Friday at 17:00 is due for acknowledgement on Monday at 08:15 (R-14's "around the clock" rejected).

**Reason:** R-14 exists because a P1 means the whole organisation has stopped work. An SLA that lets a
Friday-evening outage wait until Monday measures nothing the customer cares about, and it makes the one target
with a pager behind it meaningless for 128 of the 168 hours in a week. Narrowing R-13 to P2 to P4 keeps its
purpose, which is not to penalise the desk for hours it is not staffed for routine work, while keeping the
single promise that justifies an on-call rota. It also matches how the desk is staffed: on-call covers P1
only, so a wall-clock target for P2 to P4 would generate breaches nobody is rostered to prevent.

[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C1 - SLA clock for P1
**Service owner:** The Service Desk Manager, who owns the incident management practice, staffs the P1 on-call
rota and signs the SLA with the business; the Service Level Manager countersigns the target table.

**Customer outcome:** A P1 raised on Friday at 17:00 is acknowledged by 17:15 and worked until resolved; the
customer whose organisation has stopped is never told to wait for Monday. Customers with P2 to P4 issues get
the published business-hours targets, which are the ones the desk can actually staff and report on honestly.

[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C3 - VIP reporters and the priority matrix
**Decision:** After the matrix, a ticket whose reporter has vip = true and that landed on P3 or P4 is raised
to P2; P1 and P2 are unchanged. The minimal conflicting part of R-05, the words "from nothing else", is
narrowed to "from nothing the client sends as a priority": a priority field in the request is still ignored,
and neither reporter nor agent can request one. All of R-06 stands.

**Rejected alternative:** The matrix alone decides and reporter.vip is stored but ignored; VIP visibility is
handled by a queue filter on the flag (R-06's uplift rejected).

**Reason:** The purpose of R-05 is to stop reporters and agents negotiating priorities ticket by ticket. The
VIP flag is not such a negotiation: it is a standing decision by management about a small set of people whose
blocked work has an outsized business cost, and it is maintained by the desk, not chosen by the reporter.
Capping the uplift at P2 keeps P1 reserved for genuine organisation-wide impact, so the on-call rota is never
paged for an executive's cosmetic issue, while the ticket reaches the desk board within the hour, which is the
whole point of R-06.

student.question: By how much were the clock-skewed commits later than the deployment that shipped them?
student.answer: The clock-skewed commits were later than the deployment by between 30 seconds and 15 minutes. Source: [EDGE-CASES.md]
student.context:
[EDGE-CASES.md]
Edge cases in the practice event log > E1 - clock skew produces a negative lead time
- What the log contains: three commits whose `at` is later than the deployment that shipped them, by between
  thirty seconds and fifteen minutes. Two machines disagreed about the time, which is the ordinary cause.
- What a default definition would have done: `max(0, ...)` is rare; dropping the pair is common, and so is
  reporting a negative median. Dropping is the dangerous one, because it is silent.
- Why the rule is defensible: a clamped pair keeps the deployment in the denominator, so the median is not
  biased upward by discarding exactly the fastest-looking observations, and the anomaly count makes the
  measurement problem visible instead of hiding it inside a metric nobody questions.

[EDGE-CASES.md]
Edge cases in the practice event log > E4 - a deployment with zero linked commits
- What the log contains: four production deployments whose `commits` list is empty - a configuration rollout,
  a re-run of a failed job, and the two the failure injections produced.
- What a default definition would have done: drop the deployment (which understates deployment frequency and
  the change fail rate denominator) or divide by zero computing its lead time.
- Why the rule is defensible: a deployment happened, so deployment frequency must count it, and if it failed,
  the change fail rate must count it too. What it cannot do is contribute a lead time, because there is no
  commit to measure from. The two facts live in different metrics and the rule keeps them apart.

[EDGE-CASES.md]
Edge cases in the practice event log > E2 - a revert of a revert
- What the log contains: two chains where a commit reverts a commit that is itself a revert. Under R-06 both
  revert commits inherit the original change, so three commits are one change.
- What a default definition would have done: count commits, not changes, and report three changes where there
  is one; or treat every revert as evidence of a failed change and inflate the rework rate.
- Why the rule is defensible: the unit DORA measures is a change that reaches users, and reverting a revert
  puts the original change back. Counting the round trip as three changes would reward churn, which is
  precisely the behaviour the instability metrics exist to detect.

student.question: What is the availability error budget of the /kb/search SLO in minutes?
student.answer: The availability error budget of the /kb/search SLO is 201.6 minutes. Source: [slo.md]
student.context:
[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Availability
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered without a 5xx. **SLO**: 99.5 % over 28 days.
**Error budget**: 0.5 % of requests, which at a steady rate is 201.6 minutes of total outage in the window.

The dependency itself fails about 0.16 % of the time (measured: 4 errors in 2,400 requests, and the profile's own
rate); a 99.9 % objective would leave a budget of 0.1 % that `kb-index` alone overspends every day, so every alert on
it would page for a failure nobody on this team can fix. 99.5 % leaves the dependency's normal failures at a burn
rate of about 0.3 and still pages when a real incident multiplies them.

[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Latency
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered within 0.3 s, counted from the histogram's `le="0.3"` bucket -
a boundary of the ladder, so the SLI is a count, not an interpolation. **SLO**: 99 % over 28 days.
**Error budget**: 1 % of requests, 403.2 minutes.

Measured with the published command, the p99 is about 236 ms and the p99.9 about 265 ms: the slow requests are a
narrow mode near 230 ms (about 3 % of requests), not a long tail. A threshold at the p99 would spend the whole budget
on the dependency's normal behaviour; 0.3 s sits above that mode, so a healthy service burns well under 1 % and the
budget is spent only when the slow mode moves or grows.

[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > front matter

  service: svcdesk
  route: /kb/search
  window: 28d
  slis:
    availability:
      objective: 0.995
      good: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search", http_response_status_code!~"5.."}[5m]))'
      valid: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search"}[5m]))'
      error_budget: {fraction: 0.005, minutes: 201.6}

      threshold_seconds: 0.3

student.question: How many boundaries does the latency histogram's bucket ladder have?
student.answer: The latency histogram's bucket ladder has 23 boundaries. Source: [slo.md]
student.context:
[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Buckets
The ladder (`src/svcdesk/metrics.py`) is coarse below 150 ms, a boundary every 10 ms from 180 ms to 280 ms, and 0.3 s
exact for the SLI: 23 boundaries. At q = 236 ms the containing bucket is (0.23, 0.24], 4 % of q; the checker's q
differs from a laptop's by a few per cent, which the 10 ms steps absorb on either side.

[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Latency
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered within 0.3 s, counted from the histogram's `le="0.3"` bucket -
a boundary of the ladder, so the SLI is a count, not an interpolation. **SLO**: 99 % over 28 days.
**Error budget**: 1 % of requests, 403.2 minutes.

Measured with the published command, the p99 is about 236 ms and the p99.9 about 265 ms: the slow requests are a
narrow mode near 230 ms (about 3 % of requests), not a long tail. A threshold at the p99 would spend the whole budget
on the dependency's normal behaviour; 0.3 s sits above that mode, so a healthy service burns well under 1 % and the
budget is spent only when the slow mode moves or grows.

[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
- Size: the instructor's partition was 713,133 bytes for 10,792 rows, about 66 bytes a row; my rows carry one more
  short column (`org`), so a 500-row bucket is a few tens of KB, far from the 1 MB partition threshold. Rows, not
  bytes, are the binding limit.

**What `day` does and does not do.** Every event of a slice has the same UTC day, so `day` divides nothing inside a
window: without the bucket, the bot's 12,000 events would still be one partition. What `day` bounds is growth over
time: a real table keeps every day, and without `day` an actor's partition would grow for as long as the actor
exists. The bucket bounds the window; the day bounds the calendar.

**What a bucket costs the reader.** `bucket IN :buckets` reads 24 partitions to answer one actor's window (3 for a
repository), and at RF 3 each of them can live on another node: more coordinator work and more requests than a
single-partition read. That is why I stopped at the smallest B my rule allows rather than taking 32 or 100.

student.question: How much did the recommendation service's resident memory grow during the incident?
student.answer: The recommendation service's resident memory grew from 73.0 MB to 76.0 MB during the incident. Source: [postmortem.md]
student.context:
[postmortem.md]
Postmortem: one order in twelve failed and product pages broke for eight minutes > Impact
  longer than 5 s in shipping and in checkout (`calls_total - duration_milliseconds_bucket{le="5000"}`, 0 before
  and 1 after). Checkout's p95 crossed 3 s for one minute (CheckoutLatencyHigh, 23:12:09 to 23:12:59).
- **Recommendations without cache**: no visible user impact within the eight minutes; recommendation's resident
  memory grew from 73.0 MB to 76.0 MB (`process_runtime_cpython_memory_bytes{service_name="recommendation",type="rss"}`)
  and its p95 stayed under 10 ms.

[postmortem.md]
Postmortem: one order in twelve failed and product pages broke for eight minutes > Root Causes
Three flags of the demo's flag provider switched to failing values together. productCatalogFailure made
product-catalog answer GetProduct with an error for one product of the catalogue, so every order and every product
page containing that product failed. intlShippingSlowdown (variant 10sec) made shipping's ShipOrder ten seconds
slower for non-US addresses, which slowed the orders that shipped abroad. recommendationCacheFailure disabled the
recommendation service's cache, a resource fault whose memory and latency growth had not become visible when it was
switched off. What was already wrong: flags that can fail production paths are switchable at runtime by a source
that overrides the shop's own flag file, with no change record and no alert that names them.

[postmortem.md]
Postmortem: one order in twelve failed and product pages broke for eight minutes > Summary
From 23:07:36 to 23:15:31 UTC three feature flags failed at once. Product-catalog's GetProduct failed for one product
in ten, which failed one order in twelve and broke product and recommendation pages; non-US orders slowed by ten
seconds in shipping; and the recommendation service ran without its cache. Switching the three flags off restored
service within eight minutes of the onset.

student.question: What precision and recall did Semgrep reach in the bake-off?
student.answer: Semgrep reached a precision of 0.80 and a recall of 0.40 in the bake-off. Source: [TRIAGE.md]
student.context:
[TRIAGE.md]
Triage > Bake-off
Gate choice: keep Trivy (dependency files and image) and gitleaks as the gates, as the skeleton does. On my set
their dependency findings are exact (precision 1.0 on the pins), and a red gate has a cheap, obvious fix. Their
secret findings are less clean (0.67-0.75 precision because of the fixture), which is acceptable only because
.gitleaksignore offers a reasoned, expiring way out. Semgrep (0.80) and the AI reviewer (0.78) belong in review
comments, not in the gate: one false alarm in five would teach people to click through red builds, and the AI's
errors are about lines, which a human reviewer forgives and a gate cannot. Every recall here is an upper bound -
seeded defects are written to be found, the set is 10 defects small, and A12 shows the class all five scanners
miss by construction.

[TRIAGE.md]
Triage > Bake-off
The three dependency scanners find both pins and nothing else, with no false alarm: Trivy's 20, Grype's 18 and
OSV-Scanner's 36 raw results collapse onto 2 defects. Trivy's third TP and its one FP come from its secret scanner
(the GitHub PAT, and a JWT in app/token_fixtures.py). That JWT is the surprise cell: gitleaks, Semgrep and Trivy all
flag it, and the key says it is a decoy - a test fixture, not a credential. Every secret detector paid one FP for it,
and gitleaks and Trivy both missed the SMTP password in config/mailer.py, a plain string assignment with no
recognisable token shape. Semgrep found three of the five code defects (shell=True, yaml.load, eval) and missed the
path traversal and the access-control defect. The local AI reviewer has the best recall (0.70) but its two FPs are

student.question: How long would the gate's 150 searches take at a first step of 1 %?
student.answer: The gate's 150 searches would take 375 seconds at a first step of 1 %. Source: [corpus/checkpoint/lab6/BLAST-RADIUS.md]
student.context:
[corpus/checkpoint/lab6/BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Postmortem action
The first step is 10 %, not the 1 % of the action item, and that is arithmetic rather than neglect. The shop's 1 %
was sized for the shop's traffic; here 1 % of 40 searches a second is 0.4 a second, so the gate's 150 searches would
take 375 s, over twice the 170 s deadline, and even the 20 searches before any bad share is judged take 50 s. What
carries over is the principle - a first exposure small enough that the gate knows before many users do - and its
measure is the number of users a bad step can hurt: in the six flag runs above, 0 for the honest candidate and 23,
33, 53 and 71 for the bad ones, all rolled back by the flag alone, against the 150 a release may cost.

[corpus/checkpoint/lab6/BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Gate
What the empty-data case decides. **No data never passes**: a step needs its `min_duration` and `min_requests: 150`
searches it counted itself. A hung candidate answers at most 120 searches before it stops, so it can never collect
150, and because it is not observed at all, its 5xx and latency shares look perfect. What catches it is the collapse
rule: over a 15 s window (three scrapes), the candidate's share of all processed searches must be at least a quarter
of what its weight sends it (2.5 % at weight 10, 12.5 % at 50 %, and 12.5 % in the shadow, where it should process a
copy of every search, i.e. half of all). If Prometheus has no searches at all over the window, the phase fails too;
a read Prometheus does not answer is a missed read, never zero. The window lies inside every phase (steps last 45 s
and 20 s), and the shadow needs 200 copies, more than the 120 after which a hang stops: a hang can pass neither.

[corpus/checkpoint/lab6/BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Gate
The baseline is the checkpoint `slo.md` (`itsmlab.yaml`: `baselines: {lab3: checkpoint}`): availability 99.5 % and
latency 99 % under 0.3 s, both over 28 days. Their error budgets are 0.5 % and 1 % of the searches. The gate's
thresholds are burn rates of those budgets: with `max_burn_rate: 10` on both, a phase fails when more than
**10 x 0.5 % = 5 %** of the candidate's searches answer 5xx, or more than **10 x 1 % = 10 %** take longer than 0.3 s.
That is far below what a bad candidate does (every one reaches at least 30 %: burn 60 on availability, 30 on latency)
and far above what an honest one does: over the steps of the 17 honest runs the candidates answered 12 of 8,796
searches with a 5xx (0.14 %, `kb-index`'s own failures: burn 0.3) and none took over 0.3 s on the `itsm-reference`
profile.

student.question: About how many bytes per row did the instructor's hot partition take?
student.answer: The instructor's hot partition took about 66 bytes per row. Source: [EVIDENCE.md]
student.context:
[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Guardrails
(1 rows)
```

Before the flush the same query answered `(0 rows)`: the 66,249 rows were still in the memtables, and the
large-data records are written into an SSTable's metadata when the SSTable is written, so there was nothing to
read yet. After `nodetool flush instructor` on all three nodes every node lists the partition, because with RF 3 on
three nodes each node holds a full replica and judges only its own SSTables. The 10,792 rows are exactly
`github-actions[bot]`'s events in the slice (`itsmlab slice 7` printed the same number): one partition per actor
puts every event of the bot in one partition, ten times the 1,000-row threshold, in 713,133 bytes (about 66 bytes a
row, so this partition is convicted for rows, not yet for size).

[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
- Size: the instructor's partition was 713,133 bytes for 10,792 rows, about 66 bytes a row; my rows carry one more
  short column (`org`), so a 500-row bucket is a few tens of KB, far from the 1 MB partition threshold. Rows, not
  bytes, are the binding limit.

**What `day` does and does not do.** Every event of a slice has the same UTC day, so `day` divides nothing inside a
window: without the bucket, the bot's 12,000 events would still be one partition. What `day` bounds is growth over
time: a real table keeps every day, and without `day` an actor's partition would grow for as long as the actor
exists. The bucket bounds the window; the day bounds the calendar.

**What a bucket costs the reader.** `bucket IN :buckets` reads 24 partitions to answer one actor's window (3 for a
repository), and at RF 3 each of them can live on another node: more coordinator work and more requests than a
single-partition read. That is why I stopped at the smallest B my rule allows rather than taking 32 or 100.

[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
**`events_by_ticket` needs no bucket.** A ticket has at most four phases (`created`, `acknowledged`, `resolved`,
`closed`), so its partition holds at most four rows, plus one more pair per reopen; nothing D-05 bounds makes a
ticket's partition grow, so the arithmetic is 4 against 1,000.

| table | partition key | clustering columns | B | rows per partition at D-05's bound | against 1,000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `events_by_repo` | `(repo, day, bucket)` | `created_at, event_id` | 3 | 1,500 / 3 = 500, sd about 18 | 500 rows of margin, about 27 sd |
| `events_by_actor` | `(actor, day, bucket)` | `created_at, event_id` | 24 | 12,000 / 24 = 500, sd about 22 | 500 rows of margin, about 23 sd |
| `events_by_ticket` | `(ticket_id)` | `at, phase` | - | at most 4 (one per phase) | far below |

what `deploy.config.yaml` says and why. Every run quoted here is the course's traffic (40 searches a second, 1 s

Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Gate
How many searches before a bad share can be told from that floor. The gate judges a share only over at least 20
canary searches and only when at least 12 of them were bad (the two fixed guards in `deploy.sh`), and it looks every
5 s - 20 searches a look at weight 10. For this profile any bad count would do; the 12 is for the slowest kb-index
profile the course has, with 4.5 % of its searches over the threshold. With at least 5 bad, such an honest candidate
would be rolled back in 4.8 % of runs (exact binomial over the looks of both steps: 5/40 is already 12.5 %); with 12,
in 0.73 %. A candidate at the lowest bad share the images draw (30 %) is then caught by the second look (40 searches)
with probability 0.56, by the third with 0.97 and by the fourth with 0.999 - and still by the fifth with 0.99 at the
loosest threshold R-09 allows (20 %). Measured, the 12 costs nothing visible: the first look that sees 20 searches
usually sees 30 with 12-16 bad among them (errors q 0.31-0.32: 14, 27 and 19 failed requests with 12; 15, 13 and 25
with 5).

Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release
`deploy.sh` releases one candidate at a time through `release/compose.yml`: Caddy (`edge`) splits the users'
searches by weight between the stable build, the candidate and `shadow`, an nginx that answers from the stable build
and copies each search to the candidate; a gate reads the candidate's own SLIs from Prometheus. The numbers below are
what `deploy.config.yaml` says and why. Every run quoted here is the course's traffic (40 searches a second, 1 s
patience from the scheduled instant) through this stack, on 30 September 2026, with the TEST-key images and the
practice seeds `p01`..`p16`.

[corpus/checkpoint/lab6/BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Gate
How many searches before a bad share can be told from that floor. The gate judges a share only over at least 20
canary searches and only when at least 12 of them were bad (the two fixed guards in `deploy.sh`), and it looks every
5 s - 20 searches a look at weight 10. For this profile any bad count would do; the 12 is for the slowest kb-index
profile the course has, with 4.5 % of its searches over the threshold. With at least 5 bad, such an honest candidate
would be rolled back in 4.8 % of runs (exact binomial over the looks of both steps: 5/40 is already 12.5 %); with 12,
in 0.73 %. A candidate at the lowest bad share the images draw (30 %) is then caught by the second look (40 searches)
with probability 0.56, by the third with 0.97 and by the fourth with 0.999 - and still by the fifth with 0.99 at the
loosest threshold R-09 allows (20 %). Measured, the 12 costs nothing visible: the first look that sees 20 searches
usually sees 30 with 12-16 bad among them (errors q 0.31-0.32: 14, 27 and 19 failed requests with 12; 15, 13 and 25
with 5).

[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C3 - VIP reporters and the priority matrix
**Service owner:** The Service Desk Manager, who owns the desk's queue policy and maintains the VIP list
together with the business relationship manager; the Service Level Manager is informed because P2 volumes
change.

**Customer outcome:** An executive's blocked laptop is seen within the hour instead of by the end of the day,
without displacing an organisation-wide outage; every other reporter keeps the published matrix and can see
exactly why a ticket has the priority it has.

[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search`
The service owner is the service desk team; the customer outcome is an agent who finds the known-error article while
the caller is still on the line. Both SLIs count requests, not minutes: a slow search that nobody made costs nothing.

[specs/spec.md]
Feature specification: svcdesk, the service-desk API > User stories
1. As a reporter I raise a ticket with a title, a description, my name, and the impact and urgency of the
   incident, and I get back a ticket with an id, a computed priority and two SLA deadlines.
2. As a desk agent I move a ticket through acknowledged, in progress, resolved and closed, and the service
   records when each step happened.
3. As a reporter whose fix did not work I reopen a resolved ticket within seven days (and a closed one, if the
   desk's policy allows it) and the ticket goes back to in progress.
4. As a service level manager I ask at any instant whether a ticket's acknowledgement or resolution target is
   breached and whether its clock is currently paused.
5. As the checker I drive the service with a per-request test clock so that every scenario is reproducible.

[corpus/checkpoint/lab6/BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Blast radius
Why not the plans that are shorter to write, each measured on the same day with the same gate: **100 % at once**
cost 125 and 119 for errors and slow at q 0.31 and 0.32 (under the ceiling only because the gate reacted in 10 s;
R-22 fails it anyway) and 698-768 for a hang; **25 % first** cost 46 (errors), 41 (slow) and 120-154 for a hang,
straddling the ceiling; **a 60 s window** cost 185-214 for a hang; **no collapse rule** let the hang run to the
deadline, 508-604; **a gate that passes on empty data** promoted the hang, 1,079-1,146 and no outcome; **weights
`0 0` on rollback** turned an errors rollback into an outage, 636-643 and no outcome.

[TRIAGE.md]
Triage > Bake-off
The three dependency scanners find both pins and nothing else, with no false alarm: Trivy's 20, Grype's 18 and
OSV-Scanner's 36 raw results collapse onto 2 defects. Trivy's third TP and its one FP come from its secret scanner
(the GitHub PAT, and a JWT in app/token_fixtures.py). That JWT is the surprise cell: gitleaks, Semgrep and Trivy all
flag it, and the key says it is a decoy - a test fixture, not a credential. Every secret detector paid one FP for it,
and gitleaks and Trivy both missed the SMTP password in config/mailer.py, a plain string assignment with no
recognisable token shape. Semgrep found three of the five code defects (shell=True, yaml.load, eval) and missed the
path traversal and the access-control defect. The local AI reviewer has the best recall (0.70) but its two FPs are
both near-misses: on attachment_export.py it called the shell injection on line 11 a path traversal on lines 6-8,
and on attachment_read.py it put the right class on lines 6-8 instead of 9-10 - a 4B model miscounting lines in a
diff. Nobody found A12, the missing ownership check: no pattern matcher sees what is absent.

[corpus/checkpoint/lab6/BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Gate
What the empty-data case decides. **No data never passes**: a step needs its `min_duration` and `min_requests: 150`
searches it counted itself. A hung candidate answers at most 120 searches before it stops, so it can never collect
150, and because it is not observed at all, its 5xx and latency shares look perfect. What catches it is the collapse
rule: over a 15 s window (three scrapes), the candidate's share of all processed searches must be at least a quarter
of what its weight sends it (2.5 % at weight 10, 12.5 % at 50 %, and 12.5 % in the shadow, where it should process a
copy of every search, i.e. half of all). If Prometheus has no searches at all over the window, the phase fails too;
a read Prometheus does not answer is a missed read, never zero. The window lies inside every phase (steps last 45 s
and 20 s), and the shadow needs 200 copies, more than the 120 after which a hang stops: a hang can pass neither.

a read Prometheus does not answer is a missed read, never zero. The window lies inside every phase (steps last 45 s
and 20 s), and the shadow needs 200 copies, more than the 120 after which a hang stops: a hang can pass neither.

skip-top.question: By how much were the clock-skewed commits later than the deployment that shipped them?
skip-top.answer:
I don't know - the excerpts do not say.

Source: [EDGE-CASES.md]
skip-top.context:
[EDGE-CASES.md]
Edge cases in the practice event log > E5 - a deployment that failed and never recovered
- What the log contains: one failed production deployment whose incident is still open at the end of the log.
- What a default definition would have done: treat the window's end as the recovery instant, which invents a
  number, or drop the deployment entirely, which quietly improves the change fail rate.
- Why the rule is defensible: an unrecovered failure has no recovery time, and inventing one would make the
  recovery median better the longer an incident stays open. Reporting it as an open failure and still counting
  it in the change fail rate keeps the bad news in exactly one place where it cannot be diluted.

[EDGE-CASES.md]
Edge cases in the practice event log > E3 - a hotfix that never touched `main`
- What the log contains: four commits on `hotfix/...` branches that were deployed straight to production, as
  hotfixes are. They never appear on `main` and never will.
- What a default definition would have done: filter commits on `branch == "main"`, which is what every tutorial
  query does, and lose the hotfixes - the very changes most worth measuring.
- Why the rule is defensible: the question the metric asks is how long a change took to reach production, and a
  hotfix reached production. A branch name is a workflow convention, not a fact about delivery.

[postmortem.md]
Postmortem: one order in twelve failed and product pages broke for eight minutes > Root Causes
Three flags of the demo's flag provider switched to failing values together. productCatalogFailure made
product-catalog answer GetProduct with an error for one product of the catalogue, so every order and every product
page containing that product failed. intlShippingSlowdown (variant 10sec) made shipping's ShipOrder ten seconds
slower for non-US addresses, which slowed the orders that shipped abroad. recommendationCacheFailure disabled the
recommendation service's cache, a resource fault whose memory and latency growth had not become visible when it was
switched off. What was already wrong: flags that can fail production paths are switchable at runtime by a source
that overrides the shop's own flag file, with no change record and no alert that names them.

skip-top.question: What is the availability error budget of the /kb/search SLO in minutes?
skip-top.answer:
The availability error budget of the /kb/search SLO is 5% of a month's budget in six hours, which is 180 minutes.

Source: [slo.md]
skip-top.context:
[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search`
The service owner is the service desk team; the customer outcome is an agent who finds the known-error article while
the caller is still on the line. Both SLIs count requests, not minutes: a slow search that nobody made costs nothing.

[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Alerts
The Workbook's multiwindow, multi-burn-rate pair on the latency SLI (`prometheus/alerts.yml`):

| alert | burn rate | long / short window | budget spent when it fires | severity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KbSearchLatencyBurnFast | 14.4 | 1h / 5m | 2 % in an hour | P1: page |
| KbSearchLatencyBurnSlow | 6 | 6h / 30m | 5 % in six hours | P2: chat |

The short windows make each alert stop within minutes of the burn stopping (test 5 in `alerts_test.yml`). The slow
burn does not wake anyone: five per cent of a month's budget in six hours can wait for the morning, and routing it to
chat is the decision that keeps the pager for the fast burn.

[slo.md]
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Buckets
The ladder (`src/svcdesk/metrics.py`) is coarse below 150 ms, a boundary every 10 ms from 180 ms to 280 ms, and 0.3 s
exact for the SLI: 23 boundaries. At q = 236 ms the containing bucket is (0.23, 0.24], 4 % of q; the checker's q
differs from a laptop's by a few per cent, which the 10 ms steps absorb on either side.

skip-top.question: How many boundaries does the latency histogram's bucket ladder have?
skip-top.answer: The latency histogram's bucket ladder has 10 boundaries. Source: [corpus/checkpoint/lab6/BLAST-RADIUS.md]
skip-top.context:
[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
**Buckets, against D-05, not against the practice slice.** My rule: B is the smallest number that keeps the
*average* bucket at D-05's bound at or below 500 rows, half the 1,000-row threshold, so that a bucket would need
twice its share to be convicted. With `bucket = event_id mod B` an actor's n events fall into B buckets as a
binomial: average n / B, standard deviation sqrt(n x (1/B) x (1 - 1/B)).

[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
**Keys.** `events_by_actor` is `PRIMARY KEY ((actor, day, bucket), created_at, event_id)`: the `WHERE` names every
partition-key column - `actor` and `day` with `=`, `bucket` with `IN` over all B values - so the coordinator knows
exactly which B partitions to read, and `created_at` is the first clustering column, so the half-open window
`[from_ts, to_ts)` is a slice of each partition's sorted rows: no `ALLOW FILTERING`. `event_id` is the last
clustering column because many events share a second (21 of the bot's in the first two seconds of the slice), and
without it they would overwrite each other. `events_by_repo` is the same with `repo` in place of `actor`.
`events_by_ticket` is `PRIMARY KEY ((ticket_id), at, phase)`: one partition per ticket; `at` alone is not unique,
because my `svcdesk` stamps `created`, `acknowledged` and `resolved` with the same second when they come quickly
(my own ticket did: three events, all at 22:57:01), so `phase` is in the key too. `ticket_id` is `text`: my ids are
UUID strings, and `text` takes any id the stream sends.

[corpus/checkpoint/lab6/BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Gate
The baseline is the checkpoint `slo.md` (`itsmlab.yaml`: `baselines: {lab3: checkpoint}`): availability 99.5 % and
latency 99 % under 0.3 s, both over 28 days. Their error budgets are 0.5 % and 1 % of the searches. The gate's
thresholds are burn rates of those budgets: with `max_burn_rate: 10` on both, a phase fails when more than
**10 x 0.5 % = 5 %** of the candidate's searches answer 5xx, or more than **10 x 1 % = 10 %** take longer than 0.3 s.
That is far below what a bad candidate does (every one reaches at least 30 %: burn 60 on availability, 30 on latency)
and far above what an honest one does: over the steps of the 17 honest runs the candidates answered 12 of 8,796
searches with a 5xx (0.14 %, `kb-index`'s own failures: burn 0.3) and none took over 0.3 s on the `itsm-reference`
profile.

twice its share to be convicted. With `bucket = event_id mod B` an actor's n events fall into B buckets as a
binomial: average n / B, standard deviation sqrt(n x (1/B) x (1 - 1/B)).

Lab 7 evidence > Model
**Keys.** `events_by_actor` is `PRIMARY KEY ((actor, day, bucket), created_at, event_id)`: the `WHERE` names every
partition-key column - `actor` and `day` with `=`, `bucket` with `IN` over all B values - so the coordinator knows
exactly which B partitions to read, and `created_at` is the first clustering column, so the half-open window
`[from_ts, to_ts)` is a slice of each partition's sorted rows: no `ALLOW FILTERING`. `event_id` is the last
clustering column because many events share a second (21 of the bot's in the first two seconds of the slice), and
without it they would overwrite each other. `events_by_repo` is the same with `repo` in place of `actor`.
`events_by_ticket` is `PRIMARY KEY ((ticket_id), at, phase)`: one partition per ticket; `at` alone is not unique,
because my `svcdesk` stamps `created`, `acknowledged` and `resolved` with the same second when they come quickly
(my own ticket did: three events, all at 22:57:01), so `phase` is in the key too. `ticket_id` is `text`: my ids are
UUID strings, and `text` takes any id the stream sends.

skip-top.context:
[corpus/checkpoint/lab6/BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Gate
How many searches before a bad share can be told from that floor. The gate judges a share only over at least 20
canary searches and only when at least 12 of them were bad (the two fixed guards in `deploy.sh`), and it looks every
5 s - 20 searches a look at weight 10. For this profile any bad count would do; the 12 is for the slowest kb-index
profile the course has, with 4.5 % of its searches over the threshold. With at least 5 bad, such an honest candidate
would be rolled back in 4.8 % of runs (exact binomial over the looks of both steps: 5/40 is already 12.5 %); with 12,
in 0.73 %. A candidate at the lowest bad share the images draw (30 %) is then caught by the second look (40 searches)
with probability 0.56, by the third with 0.97 and by the fourth with 0.999 - and still by the fifth with 0.99 at the
loosest threshold R-09 allows (20 %). Measured, the 12 costs nothing visible: the first look that sees 20 searches
usually sees 30 with 12-16 bad among them (errors q 0.31-0.32: 14, 27 and 19 failed requests with 12; 15, 13 and 25
with 5).

[corpus/checkpoint/lab6/BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Change classification
Risk is **low** because exposure is bounded before anything is known (copies first; then 10 % of the searches until
150 have been judged), detection is fast (8-18 s for a bad share of 30 % or more, 11-15 s for a hang), and recovery
is one admin-API call that the stable build, which never stops, absorbs at once.

The autonomy classes in every record follow Lecture 6's ladder. Everything the script changes - starting the
candidate, the weights, the shadow, the flag, promoting, rolling back - is **closed-loop**: the gate decides and the
script acts, because no human is there to ask. Everything it reads to decide - the candidate's build and every gate
phase's readings from Prometheus - is **read-only**. Nothing is `suggest` or `approve-then-act`: an approval inside
the run cannot exist, and one before it is the standard change itself. What keeps closed-loop safe here is that the
loop can only move towards the stable build without a passed gate: any unexpected error rolls back, and a rollback
that fails exits 1, which the runner records as a run without an outcome instead of a claimed one.

[corpus/checkpoint/lab6/BLAST-RADIUS.md]
Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Blast radius
"Canary only" is this script with `shadow: null`, the Core release every student builds; D runs from the first
user search the candidate answered (a hang: from its last answer) to the script's exit. The estimate holds within a
few requests in every run, and it says where the budget goes: D is 8-18 s for a bad share (the first look with 20
searches, plus one scrape and one look of lag) and 11-15 s for a hang (the collapse window). At weight 10 the worst
run cost 54 of the ceiling's 150; the ceiling allows D up to 150 / (40 x 0.1) = 37 s for a hang, room for a window of
about 30 s. With the shadow, no bad candidate answered a single user search (R-29), and the release takes 88-92 s to
promote, 12-25 s to roll back.

skip-top.context:
[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
**`events_by_ticket` needs no bucket.** A ticket has at most four phases (`created`, `acknowledged`, `resolved`,
`closed`), so its partition holds at most four rows, plus one more pair per reopen; nothing D-05 bounds makes a
ticket's partition grow, so the arithmetic is 4 against 1,000.

| table | partition key | clustering columns | B | rows per partition at D-05's bound | against 1,000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `events_by_repo` | `(repo, day, bucket)` | `created_at, event_id` | 3 | 1,500 / 3 = 500, sd about 18 | 500 rows of margin, about 27 sd |
| `events_by_actor` | `(actor, day, bucket)` | `created_at, event_id` | 24 | 12,000 / 24 = 500, sd about 22 | 500 rows of margin, about 23 sd |
| `events_by_ticket` | `(ticket_id)` | `at, phase` | - | at most 4 (one per phase) | far below |

[EVIDENCE.md]
Lab 7 evidence > Model
**Keys.** `events_by_actor` is `PRIMARY KEY ((actor, day, bucket), created_at, event_id)`: the `WHERE` names every
partition-key column - `actor` and `day` with `=`, `bucket` with `IN` over all B values - so the coordinator knows
exactly which B partitions to read, and `created_at` is the first clustering column, so the half-open window
`[from_ts, to_ts)` is a slice of each partition's sorted rows: no `ALLOW FILTERING`. `event_id` is the last
clustering column because many events share a second (21 of the bot's in the first two seconds of the slice), and
without it they would overwrite each other. `events_by_repo` is the same with `repo` in place of `actor`.
`events_by_ticket` is `PRIMARY KEY ((ticket_id), at, phase)`: one partition per ticket; `at` alone is not unique,
because my `svcdesk` stamps `created`, `acknowledged` and `resolved` with the same second when they come quickly
(my own ticket did: three events, all at 22:57:01), so `phase` is in the key too. `ticket_id` is `text`: my ids are
UUID strings, and `text` takes any id the stream sends.

[postmortem.md]
Postmortem: one order in twelve failed and product pages broke for eight minutes > Root Causes
Three flags of the demo's flag provider switched to failing values together. productCatalogFailure made
product-catalog answer GetProduct with an error for one product of the catalogue, so every order and every product
page containing that product failed. intlShippingSlowdown (variant 10sec) made shipping's ShipOrder ten seconds
slower for non-US addresses, which slowed the orders that shipped abroad. recommendationCacheFailure disabled the
recommendation service's cache, a resource fault whose memory and latency growth had not become visible when it was
switched off. What was already wrong: flags that can fail production paths are switchable at runtime by a source
that overrides the shop's own flag file, with no change record and no alert that names them.

[EDGE-CASES.md]
Edge cases in the practice event log > E3 - a hotfix that never touched `main`
- What the log contains: four commits on `hotfix/...` branches that were deployed straight to production, as
  hotfixes are. They never appear on `main` and never will.
- What a default definition would have done: filter commits on `branch == "main"`, which is what every tutorial
  query does, and lose the hotfixes - the very changes most worth measuring.
- Why the rule is defensible: the question the metric asks is how long a change took to reach production, and a
  hotfix reached production. A branch name is a workflow convention, not a fact about delivery.

Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Postmortem action
The first step is 10 %, not the 1 % of the action item, and that is arithmetic rather than neglect. The shop's 1 %
was sized for the shop's traffic; here 1 % of 40 searches a second is 0.4 a second, so the gate's 150 searches would
take 375 s, over twice the 170 s deadline, and even the 20 searches before any bad share is judged take 50 s. What
carries over is the principle - a first exposure small enough that the gate knows before many users do - and its
measure is the number of users a bad step can hurt: in the six flag runs above, 0 for the honest candidate and 23,
33, 53 and 71 for the bad ones, all rolled back by the flag alone, against the 150 a release may cost.

[specs/spec.md]
Feature specification: svcdesk, the service-desk API > Functional requirements
  network at run time, healthy within 120 s; a `tests` service under the `tests` profile. Tickets persist
  across a container restart (R-23).

[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening
**Reason:** Closure is the point where the record becomes evidence: it feeds SLA attainment reports, problem
records and the monthly service review, and a record that can silently change after that point makes every
report reproducible only by luck. The 7-day reopen window after resolution already gives the reporter the "the
fix did not work" path that R-10 is for; the resolved state exists precisely so that closure can wait until
the reporter has confirmed. A new ticket linked via related_to preserves the history of both records and gives
problem management a countable signal, how many closed tickets spawned follow-up work, instead of a mutated
one.

**Service owner:** The Incident Manager, process owner of incident management, who signs off the closure rules
because closure is what makes the incident record trustworthy for reporting and problem management.

**Customer outcome:** A reporter whose fix failed within a week reopens the resolved ticket without friction;
once the ticket is closed, the customer raises a linked ticket and the history of both is preserved, so the
reports the customer relies on (SLA attainment, recurring issues) stay true.

no-names.question: Who is the service owner of the decision on closed tickets and reopening?
no-names.answer: The service owner of the decision on closed tickets and reopening is The Incident Manager, process owner of incident management. Source: [Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening]
no-names.context:
Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening
**Decision:** A closed ticket is immutable. Reopen works from resolved only, within 7 days of resolved_at; a
reopen request on a closed ticket answers 409 whatever its age, and further work on the same issue is a new
ticket that references the closed one via related_to. The minimal conflicting part of R-10, the words "or
closed" and "or closure", is rejected; reopening a resolved ticket, the rest of R-10, stands together with all
of R-09.

**Rejected alternative:** Reopen allowed from closed as well, within 7 days of closed_at, with the record
becoming immutable only after that window.

Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening
**Reason:** Closure is the point where the record becomes evidence: it feeds SLA attainment reports, problem
records and the monthly service review, and a record that can silently change after that point makes every
report reproducible only by luck. The 7-day reopen window after resolution already gives the reporter the "the
fix did not work" path that R-10 is for; the resolved state exists precisely so that closure can wait until
the reporter has confirmed. A new ticket linked via related_to preserves the history of both records and gives
problem management a countable signal, how many closed tickets spawned follow-up work, instead of a mutated
one.

**Service owner:** The Incident Manager, process owner of incident management, who signs off the closure rules
because closure is what makes the incident record trustworthy for reporting and problem management.

**Customer outcome:** A reporter whose fix failed within a week reopens the resolved ticket without friction;
once the ticket is closed, the customer raises a linked ticket and the history of both is preserved, so the
reports the customer relies on (SLA attainment, recurring issues) stay true.

  and keeps its resolution target (R-15, R-16).

  resolved, reopen from resolved within 7 days of `resolved_at` and, under C2 = reopen only, from closed within

- FR-6 `GET /tickets` returns every matching ticket in one array, optionally filtered by `state` and
  `priority`, without pagination (R-19); `GET /tickets/{id}` returns one ticket or 404 (R-18).

The Lab 4 baseline is the checkpoint postmortem (`itsmlab.yaml`: `baselines: {lab4: checkpoint}`), whose incident
was three feature flags switched on at full strength at once: nothing stood between the flip and every user. Its
action item **ITSM-42** is "Put the payment and shipping flags behind a percentage rollout that starts at 1 %".
This repository's release has the same kind of switch - svcdesk 2.1's new code is behind the flag `svcdesk-2-1` -
and the commit named in the front matter gives it that rollout: `RELEASE_STRATEGY=flag` deploys the candidate dark
(flag off: 2.0.0's code on every search), then raises the flag through flagd's `fractional` in the steps of
`deploy.config.yaml`'s `flag:`, lets the gate judge only the searches that got `on`, and turns the flag on for
everyone only after the last step passed; any failed step turns it off for everyone within about a second. Every
change of the flag is an action in `CHANGE.md`, with its time and its autonomy class, which is the record ITSM-41
asked an alert for.

no-names.question: Under the rejected alternative, when would a P1 raised on Friday at 17:00 be due for acknowledgement?
no-names.answer: Under the rejected alternative, a P1 raised on Friday at 17:00 would be due for acknowledgement on Monday at 08:15. Source: [Decisions > C1 - SLA clock for P1]
no-names.context:
Decisions > C1 - SLA clock for P1
**Decision:** P1 acknowledgement (15 min) and resolution (4 h) run on the wall clock, around the clock; P2 to
P4 targets pause outside business hours (Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 16:00 Europe/Warsaw). The minimal
conflicting part of R-13, the words "any SLA target", is narrowed to "any P2 to P4 target"; the rest of R-13
and all of R-14 stand.

**Rejected alternative:** Every priority, including P1, pauses outside business hours, so that a P1 raised on
Friday at 17:00 is due for acknowledgement on Monday at 08:15 (R-14's "around the clock" rejected).

**Reason:** R-14 exists because a P1 means the whole organisation has stopped work. An SLA that lets a
Friday-evening outage wait until Monday measures nothing the customer cares about, and it makes the one target

no-names.question: By how much were the clock-skewed commits later than the deployment that shipped them?
no-names.answer: The clock-skewed commits were later than the deployment that shipped them by between thirty seconds and fifteen minutes. Source: [Edge cases in the practice event log > E1 - clock skew produces a negative lead time]
no-names.context:
Edge cases in the practice event log > E1 - clock skew produces a negative lead time
- What the log contains: three commits whose `at` is later than the deployment that shipped them, by between
  thirty seconds and fifteen minutes. Two machines disagreed about the time, which is the ordinary cause.
- What a default definition would have done: `max(0, ...)` is rare; dropping the pair is common, and so is
  reporting a negative median. Dropping is the dangerous one, because it is silent.
- Why the rule is defensible: a clamped pair keeps the deployment in the denominator, so the median is not
  biased upward by discarding exactly the fastest-looking observations, and the anomaly count makes the
  measurement problem visible instead of hiding it inside a metric nobody questions.

Edge cases in the practice event log > E4 - a deployment with zero linked commits
- What the log contains: four production deployments whose `commits` list is empty - a configuration rollout,
  a re-run of a failed job, and the two the failure injections produced.
- What a default definition would have done: drop the deployment (which understates deployment frequency and
  the change fail rate denominator) or divide by zero computing its lead time.
- Why the rule is defensible: a deployment happened, so deployment frequency must count it, and if it failed,
  the change fail rate must count it too. What it cannot do is contribute a lead time, because there is no
  commit to measure from. The two facts live in different metrics and the rule keeps them apart.

Edge cases in the practice event log > E2 - a revert of a revert
- What the log contains: two chains where a commit reverts a commit that is itself a revert. Under R-06 both
  revert commits inherit the original change, so three commits are one change.
- What a default definition would have done: count commits, not changes, and report three changes where there
  is one; or treat every revert as evidence of a failed change and inflate the rework rate.
- Why the rule is defensible: the unit DORA measures is a change that reaches users, and reverting a revert
  puts the original change back. Counting the round trip as three changes would reward churn, which is
  precisely the behaviour the instability metrics exist to detect.

no-names.question: What is the availability error budget of the /kb/search SLO in minutes?
no-names.answer: The availability error budget of the /kb/search SLO is 201.6 minutes. Source: [lab3_slo]
no-names.context:
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Availability
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered without a 5xx. **SLO**: 99.5 % over 28 days.
**Error budget**: 0.5 % of requests, which at a steady rate is 201.6 minutes of total outage in the window.

The dependency itself fails about 0.16 % of the time (measured: 4 errors in 2,400 requests, and the profile's own
rate); a 99.9 % objective would leave a budget of 0.1 % that `kb-index` alone overspends every day, so every alert on
it would page for a failure nobody on this team can fix. 99.5 % leaves the dependency's normal failures at a burn
rate of about 0.3 and still pages when a real incident multiplies them.

SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Latency
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered within 0.3 s, counted from the histogram's `le="0.3"` bucket -
a boundary of the ladder, so the SLI is a count, not an interpolation. **SLO**: 99 % over 28 days.
**Error budget**: 1 % of requests, 403.2 minutes.

Measured with the published command, the p99 is about 236 ms and the p99.9 about 265 ms: the slow requests are a
narrow mode near 230 ms (about 3 % of requests), not a long tail. A threshold at the p99 would spend the whole budget
on the dependency's normal behaviour; 0.3 s sits above that mode, so a healthy service burns well under 1 % and the
budget is spent only when the slow mode moves or grows.

SLO for `GET /kb/search` > front matter
lab3_slo:
  service: svcdesk
  route: /kb/search
  window: 28d
  slis:
    availability:
      objective: 0.995
      good: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search", http_response_status_code!~"5.."}[5m]))'
      valid: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search"}[5m]))'
      error_budget: {fraction: 0.005, minutes: 201.6}
    latency:
      objective: 0.99
      threshold_seconds: 0.3
      good: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search", le="0.3"}[5m]))'
      valid: 'sum(rate(http_server_request_duration_seconds_count{job="svcdesk", http_route="/kb/search"}[5m]))'
      error_budget: {fraction: 0.01, minutes: 403.2}
  alerts:
    - {alert: KbSearchLatencyBurnFast, sli: latency, burn_rate: 14.4, long_window: 1h, short_window: 5m}
    - {alert: KbSearchLatencyBurnSlow, sli: latency, burn_rate: 6, long_window: 6h, short_window: 30m}

no-names.question: What p99 and p99.9 latency did the measurement of /kb/search show?
no-names.answer: The measurement of `/kb/search` showed a p99 latency of 236 ms and a p99.9 latency of 265 ms. Source: [Lab 7 evidence]
no-names.context:
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Latency
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered within 0.3 s, counted from the histogram's `le="0.3"` bucket -
a boundary of the ladder, so the SLI is a count, not an interpolation. **SLO**: 99 % over 28 days.
**Error budget**: 1 % of requests, 403.2 minutes.

Measured with the published command, the p99 is about 236 ms and the p99.9 about 265 ms: the slow requests are a
narrow mode near 230 ms (about 3 % of requests), not a long tail. A threshold at the p99 would spend the whole budget
on the dependency's normal behaviour; 0.3 s sits above that mode, so a healthy service burns well under 1 % and the
budget is spent only when the slow mode moves or grows.

Lab 7 evidence > Stress
**Why p99 and max differ.** The p99 says 99 % of the 60,000 writes finished within 0.6 ms; the p99.9 that 60 writes
took longer than 1.9 ms; the max that the single slowest took 5.0 ms, eight times the p99. The per-second lines show
where: second 4 had its max at 5.0 ms and p99.9 3.4 ms, seconds 12, 15 and 18 had maxima of 4.1 to 4.5 ms, while
most seconds stayed under 2.5 ms. A median of 0.3 ms is one network round trip inside Docker's bridge plus a
memtable insert on two replicas; the few slow writes waited for something else - a memtable flush or a commitlog
segment switch on one of the two replicas the quorum needed, the reactor of a 1-core, overprovisioned node yielding
to the other containers on this laptop (Labs 4 and 5 were running beside the ring, load average about 3.5 on 22
cores), or the client's own thread or JVM pause. With `cl=QUORUM` the coordinator waits for the second-fastest of
three replicas, so one slow replica alone does not delay a write, but two do.

SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Alerts
The Workbook's multiwindow, multi-burn-rate pair on the latency SLI (`prometheus/alerts.yml`):

| alert | burn rate | long / short window | budget spent when it fires | severity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| KbSearchLatencyBurnFast | 14.4 | 1h / 5m | 2 % in an hour | P1: page |
| KbSearchLatencyBurnSlow | 6 | 6h / 30m | 5 % in six hours | P2: chat |

The short windows make each alert stop within minutes of the burn stopping (test 5 in `alerts_test.yml`). The slow
burn does not wake anyone: five per cent of a month's budget in six hours can wait for the morning, and routing it to
chat is the decision that keeps the pager for the fast burn.

no-names.question: How many boundaries does the latency histogram's bucket ladder have?
no-names.answer: The latency histogram's bucket ladder has 23 boundaries. Source: [SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Latency]
no-names.context:
SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Buckets
The ladder (`src/svcdesk/metrics.py`) is coarse below 150 ms, a boundary every 10 ms from 180 ms to 280 ms, and 0.3 s
exact for the SLI: 23 boundaries. At q = 236 ms the containing bucket is (0.23, 0.24], 4 % of q; the checker's q
differs from a laptop's by a few per cent, which the 10 ms steps absorb on either side.

SLO for `GET /kb/search` > Latency
**SLI**: the share of `/kb/search` requests answered within 0.3 s, counted from the histogram's `le="0.3"` bucket -
a boundary of the ladder, so the SLI is a count, not an interpolation. **SLO**: 99 % over 28 days.
**Error budget**: 1 % of requests, 403.2 minutes.

Measured with the published command, the p99 is about 236 ms and the p99.9 about 265 ms: the slow requests are a
narrow mode near 230 ms (about 3 % of requests), not a long tail. A threshold at the p99 would spend the whole budget
on the dependency's normal behaviour; 0.3 s sits above that mode, so a healthy service burns well under 1 % and the
budget is spent only when the slow mode moves or grows.

Lab 7 evidence > Model
- Size: the instructor's partition was 713,133 bytes for 10,792 rows, about 66 bytes a row; my rows carry one more
  short column (`org`), so a 500-row bucket is a few tens of KB, far from the 1 MB partition threshold. Rows, not
  bytes, are the binding limit.

**What `day` does and does not do.** Every event of a slice has the same UTC day, so `day` divides nothing inside a
window: without the bucket, the bot's 12,000 events would still be one partition. What `day` bounds is growth over
time: a real table keeps every day, and without `day` an actor's partition would grow for as long as the actor
exists. The bucket bounds the window; the day bounds the calendar.

**What a bucket costs the reader.** `bucket IN :buckets` reads 24 partitions to answer one actor's window (3 for a
repository), and at RF 3 each of them can live on another node: more coordinator work and more requests than a
single-partition read. That is why I stopped at the smallest B my rule allows rather than taking 32 or 100.

page containing that product failed. intlShippingSlowdown (variant 10sec) made shipping's ShipOrder ten seconds

switched off. What was already wrong: flags that can fail production paths are switchable at runtime by a source
that overrides the shop's own flag file, with no change record and no alert that names them.

seconds in shipping; and the recommendation service ran without its cache. Switching the three flags off restored
service within eight minutes of the onset.

no-names.question: What precision and recall did Semgrep reach in the bake-off?
no-names.answer: Semgrep reached a precision of 0.80 and a recall of 0.40 in the bake-off. Source: [folder/file.md]
no-names.context:
Triage > Bake-off
Gate choice: keep Trivy (dependency files and image) and gitleaks as the gates, as the skeleton does. On my set
their dependency findings are exact (precision 1.0 on the pins), and a red gate has a cheap, obvious fix. Their
secret findings are less clean (0.67-0.75 precision because of the fixture), which is acceptable only because
.gitleaksignore offers a reasoned, expiring way out. Semgrep (0.80) and the AI reviewer (0.78) belong in review
comments, not in the gate: one false alarm in five would teach people to click through red builds, and the AI's
errors are about lines, which a human reviewer forgives and a gate cannot. Every recall here is an upper bound -
seeded defects are written to be found, the set is 10 defects small, and A12 shows the class all five scanners
miss by construction.

Triage > Bake-off
The three dependency scanners find both pins and nothing else, with no false alarm: Trivy's 20, Grype's 18 and
OSV-Scanner's 36 raw results collapse onto 2 defects. Trivy's third TP and its one FP come from its secret scanner
(the GitHub PAT, and a JWT in app/token_fixtures.py). That JWT is the surprise cell: gitleaks, Semgrep and Trivy all
flag it, and the key says it is a decoy - a test fixture, not a credential. Every secret detector paid one FP for it,
and gitleaks and Trivy both missed the SMTP password in config/mailer.py, a plain string assignment with no
recognisable token shape. Semgrep found three of the five code defects (shell=True, yaml.load, eval) and missed the
path traversal and the access-control defect. The local AI reviewer has the best recall (0.70) but its two FPs are
both near-misses: on attachment_export.py it called the shell injection on line 11 a path traversal on lines 6-8,
and on attachment_read.py it put the right class on lines 6-8 instead of 9-10 - a 4B model miscounting lines in a
diff. Nobody found A12, the missing ownership check: no pattern matcher sees what is absent.

Triage > Bake-off
My canary set has 10 labelled defects: 5 in code (A02 shell injection, A03 path traversal, A09 yaml.load, A11 eval,
A12 a missing ownership check), 3 credentials (C03 GitHub PAT, C05 SMTP password, C06 search API key) and 2 pins
(D01 cryptography, D03 Jinja2). bakeoff.py on the receipted SARIF gives:

| tool | TP | FP | FN | precision | recall | F1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| trivy | 3 | 1 | 7 | 0.75 | 0.30 | 0.4286 |
| grype | 2 | 0 | 8 | 1.0 | 0.20 | 0.3333 |
| osv-scanner | 2 | 0 | 8 | 1.0 | 0.20 | 0.3333 |
| gitleaks | 2 | 1 | 8 | 0.6667 | 0.20 | 0.3077 |
| semgrep | 4 | 1 | 6 | 0.80 | 0.40 | 0.5333 |
| ai-reviewer (qwen3:4b-instruct, local) | 7 | 2 | 3 | 0.7778 | 0.70 | 0.7368 |

no-names.question: How long would the gate's 150 searches take at a first step of 1 %?
no-names.answer: The gate's 150 searches would take 375 seconds at a first step of 1 %. Source: [Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Postmortem action]
no-names.context:
Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Postmortem action
The first step is 10 %, not the 1 % of the action item, and that is arithmetic rather than neglect. The shop's 1 %
was sized for the shop's traffic; here 1 % of 40 searches a second is 0.4 a second, so the gate's 150 searches would
take 375 s, over twice the 170 s deadline, and even the 20 searches before any bad share is judged take 50 s. What
carries over is the principle - a first exposure small enough that the gate knows before many users do - and its
measure is the number of users a bad step can hurt: in the six flag runs above, 0 for the honest candidate and 23,
33, 53 and 71 for the bad ones, all rolled back by the flag alone, against the 150 a release may cost.

Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Gate
What the empty-data case decides. **No data never passes**: a step needs its `min_duration` and `min_requests: 150`
searches it counted itself. A hung candidate answers at most 120 searches before it stops, so it can never collect
150, and because it is not observed at all, its 5xx and latency shares look perfect. What catches it is the collapse
rule: over a 15 s window (three scrapes), the candidate's share of all processed searches must be at least a quarter
of what its weight sends it (2.5 % at weight 10, 12.5 % at 50 %, and 12.5 % in the shadow, where it should process a
copy of every search, i.e. half of all). If Prometheus has no searches at all over the window, the phase fails too;
a read Prometheus does not answer is a missed read, never zero. The window lies inside every phase (steps last 45 s
and 20 s), and the shadow needs 200 copies, more than the 120 after which a hang stops: a hang can pass neither.

Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Gate
The baseline is the checkpoint `slo.md` (`itsmlab.yaml`: `baselines: {lab3: checkpoint}`): availability 99.5 % and
latency 99 % under 0.3 s, both over 28 days. Their error budgets are 0.5 % and 1 % of the searches. The gate's
thresholds are burn rates of those budgets: with `max_burn_rate: 10` on both, a phase fails when more than
**10 x 0.5 % = 5 %** of the candidate's searches answer 5xx, or more than **10 x 1 % = 10 %** take longer than 0.3 s.
That is far below what a bad candidate does (every one reaches at least 30 %: burn 60 on availability, 30 on latency)
and far above what an honest one does: over the steps of the 17 honest runs the candidates answered 12 of 8,796
searches with a 5xx (0.14 %, `kb-index`'s own failures: burn 0.3) and none took over 0.3 s on the `itsm-reference`
profile.

no-names.question: About how many bytes per row did the instructor's hot partition take?
no-names.answer: The instructor's hot partition took about 66 bytes per row. Source: [Lab 7 evidence > Model]
no-names.context:
Lab 7 evidence > Guardrails
(1 rows)
```

Before the flush the same query answered `(0 rows)`: the 66,249 rows were still in the memtables, and the
large-data records are written into an SSTable's metadata when the SSTable is written, so there was nothing to
read yet. After `nodetool flush instructor` on all three nodes every node lists the partition, because with RF 3 on
three nodes each node holds a full replica and judges only its own SSTables. The 10,792 rows are exactly
`github-actions[bot]`'s events in the slice (`itsmlab slice 7` printed the same number): one partition per actor
puts every event of the bot in one partition, ten times the 1,000-row threshold, in 713,133 bytes (about 66 bytes a
row, so this partition is convicted for rows, not yet for size).

Lab 7 evidence > Model
- Size: the instructor's partition was 713,133 bytes for 10,792 rows, about 66 bytes a row; my rows carry one more
  short column (`org`), so a 500-row bucket is a few tens of KB, far from the 1 MB partition threshold. Rows, not
  bytes, are the binding limit.

**What `day` does and does not do.** Every event of a slice has the same UTC day, so `day` divides nothing inside a
window: without the bucket, the bot's 12,000 events would still be one partition. What `day` bounds is growth over
time: a real table keeps every day, and without `day` an actor's partition would grow for as long as the actor
exists. The bucket bounds the window; the day bounds the calendar.

**What a bucket costs the reader.** `bucket IN :buckets` reads 24 partitions to answer one actor's window (3 for a
repository), and at RF 3 each of them can live on another node: more coordinator work and more requests than a
single-partition read. That is why I stopped at the smallest B my rule allows rather than taking 32 or 100.

Lab 7 evidence > Model
**`events_by_ticket` needs no bucket.** A ticket has at most four phases (`created`, `acknowledged`, `resolved`,
`closed`), so its partition holds at most four rows, plus one more pair per reopen; nothing D-05 bounds makes a
ticket's partition grow, so the arithmetic is 4 against 1,000.

| table | partition key | clustering columns | B | rows per partition at D-05's bound | against 1,000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `events_by_repo` | `(repo, day, bucket)` | `created_at, event_id` | 3 | 1,500 / 3 = 500, sd about 18 | 500 rows of margin, about 27 sd |
| `events_by_actor` | `(actor, day, bucket)` | `created_at, event_id` | 24 | 12,000 / 24 = 500, sd about 22 | 500 rows of margin, about 23 sd |
| `events_by_ticket` | `(ticket_id)` | `at, phase` | - | at most 4 (one per phase) | far below |

no-names.question: What was svcdesk's cloud hosting bill in October 2026?
no-names.context:
Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release
`deploy.sh` releases one candidate at a time through `release/compose.yml`: Caddy (`edge`) splits the users'
searches by weight between the stable build, the candidate and `shadow`, an nginx that answers from the stable build
and copies each search to the candidate; a gate reads the candidate's own SLIs from Prometheus. The numbers below are
what `deploy.config.yaml` says and why. Every run quoted here is the course's traffic (40 searches a second, 1 s
patience from the scheduled instant) through this stack, on 30 September 2026, with the TEST-key images and the
practice seeds `p01`..`p16`.

Feature specification: svcdesk, the service-desk API > Functional requirements
  network at run time, healthy within 120 s; a `tests` service under the `tests` profile. Tickets persist
  across a container restart (R-23).

Postmortem: one order in twelve failed and product pages broke for eight minutes > Timeline
All times UTC, 10 October 2026.

- 22:51:47 - the playground starts; the injector begins its 10-minute baseline. A practice ticket at 22:52:49
  proves svcdesk's requests reach Prometheus.
- 23:02:12 - `max_over_time(ALERTS{alertstate="firing", severity="P1"}[10m])` returns nothing; no alert at all.
- 23:02:14 - the injector is armed (onset window 2 to 6 minutes).
- 23:07:36 - **onset**: the injector's fault series starts.
- 23:10:08 - ServiceLatencyRaised (shipping p95 > 1 s) pending; 23:10:09 CheckoutErrorRate pending.
- 23:11:08 - **detection**: ServiceLatencyRaised fires (P3, routed to chat, inhibited by the P1 a second later).
- 23:11:09 - CheckoutErrorRate fires (P1); 23:11:19 the page reaches the pager.
- 23:11:25 - the P1 ticket 61e3fa62-3f3f-44cc-970c-8185d6bffdff is created and **acknowledged** at 23:11:25.
- 23:11:28 - symptoms: product-catalog GetProduct, frontend product pages and recommendations, checkout PlaceOrder
  failing; shipping p95 2.6 s, checkout p95 5 s.
- 23:11:42 - what changed: `/flags.json` shows productCatalogFailure on, intlShippingSlowdown 10sec,
  recommendationCacheFailure on.
- 23:11:53 - productCatalogFailure switched off (`changed: true`).

Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release
`deploy.sh` releases one candidate at a time through `release/compose.yml`: Caddy (`edge`) splits the users'

patience from the scheduled instant) through this stack, on 30 September 2026, with the TEST-key images and the
practice seeds `p01`..`p16`.

Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Gate
How many searches before a bad share can be told from that floor. The gate judges a share only over at least 20
canary searches and only when at least 12 of them were bad (the two fixed guards in `deploy.sh`), and it looks every
5 s - 20 searches a look at weight 10. For this profile any bad count would do; the 12 is for the slowest kb-index
profile the course has, with 4.5 % of its searches over the threshold. With at least 5 bad, such an honest candidate
would be rolled back in 4.8 % of runs (exact binomial over the looks of both steps: 5/40 is already 12.5 %); with 12,
in 0.73 %. A candidate at the lowest bad share the images draw (30 %) is then caught by the second look (40 searches)
with probability 0.56, by the third with 0.97 and by the fourth with 0.999 - and still by the fifth with 0.99 at the
loosest threshold R-09 allows (20 %). Measured, the 12 costs nothing visible: the first look that sees 20 searches
usually sees 30 with 12-16 bad among them (errors q 0.31-0.32: 14, 27 and 19 failed requests with 12; 15, 13 and 25
with 5).

default-prompt.question: Who is the service owner of the decision on closed tickets and reopening?
default-prompt.answer: The service owner of the decision on closed tickets and reopening is the **Incident Manager**, who is the process owner of incident management and signs off on the closure rules.
default-prompt.context:
[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening
**Decision:** A closed ticket is immutable. Reopen works from resolved only, within 7 days of resolved_at; a
reopen request on a closed ticket answers 409 whatever its age, and further work on the same issue is a new
ticket that references the closed one via related_to. The minimal conflicting part of R-10, the words "or
closed" and "or closure", is rejected; reopening a resolved ticket, the rest of R-10, stands together with all
of R-09.

**Rejected alternative:** Reopen allowed from closed as well, within 7 days of closed_at, with the record
becoming immutable only after that window.

[DECISIONS.md]
Decisions > C2 - Closed tickets and reopening
**Reason:** Closure is the point where the record becomes evidence: it feeds SLA attainment reports, problem
records and the monthly service review, and a record that can silently change after that point makes every
report reproducible only by luck. The 7-day reopen window after resolution already gives the reporter the "the
fix did not work" path that R-10 is for; the resolved state exists precisely so that closure can wait until
the reporter has confirmed. A new ticket linked via related_to preserves the history of both records and gives
problem management a countable signal, how many closed tickets spawned follow-up work, instead of a mutated
one.

**Service owner:** The Incident Manager, process owner of incident management, who signs off the closure rules
because closure is what makes the incident record trustworthy for reporting and problem management.

**Customer outcome:** A reporter whose fix failed within a week reopens the resolved ticket without friction;
once the ticket is closed, the customer raises a linked ticket and the history of both is preserved, so the
reports the customer relies on (SLA attainment, recurring issues) stay true.

[specs/spec.md]
Feature specification: svcdesk, the service-desk API > Functional requirements
  `paused` evaluated at the request's `now`; equality is not a breach; a reopened ticket is unresolved again
  and keeps its resolution target (R-15, R-16).
- FR-5 State machine (R-07, R-08): ack from new, start from acknowledged, resolve from in_progress, close from
  resolved, reopen from resolved within 7 days of `resolved_at` and, under C2 = reopen only, from closed within

Blast radius of the svcdesk 2.1 release > Postmortem action
The Lab 4 baseline is the checkpoint postmortem (`itsmlab.yaml`: `baselines: {lab4: checkpoint}`), whose incident
was three feature flags switched on at full strength at once: nothing stood between the flip and every user. Its
action item **ITSM-42** is "Put the payment and shipping flags behind a percentage rollout that starts at 1 %".
This repository's release has the same kind of switch - svcdesk 2.1's new code is behind the flag `svcdesk-2-1` -
and the commit named in the front matter gives it that rollout: `RELEASE_STRATEGY=flag` deploys the candidate dark
(flag off: 2.0.0's code on every search), then raises the flag through flagd's `fractional` in the steps of
`deploy.config.yaml`'s `flag:`, lets the gate judge only the searches that got `on`, and turns the flag on for
everyone only after the last step passed; any failed step turns it off for everyone within about a second. Every
change of the flag is an action in `CHANGE.md`, with its time and its autonomy class, which is the record ITSM-41
asked an alert for.
